title: Stop spending money on smaller classes
gist: Noah Smith argues the US has spent decades shrinking class sizes when evidence from large meta-analyses (Filges et al. 2018; Opartny et al. 2025, 2,819 estimates from 66 studies) shows negligible effects outside small pilots like Tennessee's STAR. He contends class-size mandates such as New York's (about $1 billion for NYC) deplete the pool of good teachers, and that money should instead raise teacher pay and quality, citing Wisconsin evidence that such reforms raised test scores and were politically rewarded.

insights.claim: Smith argues American public schools generally get good value for money and American kids do well on international standardized tests, though some schools are very bad.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Pushes back on blanket 'failing schools' narratives; problems are concentrated in a subset of schools.
insights.quote: In general, American schools get pretty good value for the money they spend
insights.locator: Now, I went to public schools myself

insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Grades are becoming a weaker signal of skill, increasing the value of standardized testing for admissions and hiring.

insights.claim: Smith calls Nikole Hannah-Jones's cited EdBuild figure that nonwhite districts receive $23 billion less annually a basic math error, since total spending reflects there being many more predominantly white districts; per-student spending is what matters.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Aggregate funding-gap statistics can mislead education-policy debates and funding allocation.
insights.quote: Obviously what should matter here is spending per student, not total spending.

insights.claim: A Brookings report finds poor, predominantly nonwhite US schools get substantially more funding per student than other schools even after adjusting for local cost of living, with NYC even more lopsided, and funding for these schools has risen since 2000.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Funding levels alone are not the binding constraint for poor schools; how money is spent matters more.
insights.locator: Brookings came out with a great report

themes.theme: Teacher quantity growth and class-size mandates

insights.claim: Historically K-12 schools have hired far more teachers than administrators, and teachers per student is still rising, so administrative bloat is not the main cost driver.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Staff cost growth in education comes mainly from lowering student-teacher ratios, not overhead.
insights.quote: “Teachers per student” is still comfortably ahead, and rising
insights.locator: But historically, K-12 schools have hired

insights.claim: Per Elan Bechor, as shared by Matt Yglesias, school staff pay growth is almost entirely driven by the staff-to-student ratio rather than pay per teacher.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Budget growth has gone into headcount, not compensation, limiting teacher-quality improvement.

insights.claim: New York State passed a law mandating maximum class sizes, forcing New York City to hire many more teachers at a cost of about $1 billion to the city budget.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A large recurring budget commitment for NYC with, per Smith, little expected educational payoff.
insights.quote: at the cost of about $1 billion to the city budget
insights.locator: Major efforts to reduce class size continue.

insights.claim: Tennessee's STAR pilot (Dynarski, Hyman and Schanzenbach 2013) found small classes raised college attendance by 2.7 points, more than twice as much for Black students, 7.3 points in the poorest third of schools, and degree completion by 1.6 points.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The main positive evidence for class-size reduction comes from a small-scale pilot.
insights.quote: assignment to a small class increases students’ probability of attending college by 2.7 percentage points
insights.locator: Most prominent among these is Dynarski

insights.claim: Angrist and Lavy's 1999 Israeli Maimonides' Rule finding of class-size benefits did not hold up: their 2019 'Maimonides' Rule Redux' found precisely estimated zero effects for 2002-2011.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A landmark natural-experiment result for class size appears to have been a historical anomaly.
insights.quote: generates precisely estimated zeros in large Israeli samples for 2002-2011

insights.claim: Hoxby (2000) found zero effect from maximum class size rules, and Filges et al. (2018) meta-analysis found at best a small effect on reading and a negative but insignificant effect on math.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Systematic evidence undercuts the policy rationale for class-size spending.
insights.quote: Overall, the evidence suggests at best a small effect on reading achievement.
insights.locator: That would be consistent with the finding of Hoxby

insights.claim: Opartny et al. (2025), using 2,819 estimates from 66 studies, find class-size effects negligible for all identification approaches except Tennessee's STAR and all contexts except classes of fewer than 15 students.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The largest meta-analysis suggests class-size reductions in typical ranges deliver essentially no achievement gains.
insights.quote: The implied class size effect is negligible for all identification approaches except Tennessee’s Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio project

insights.claim: Scaled-up programs disappoint: Chingos (2012) found Florida's statewide class-size mandate had little if any effect, while Jepsen and Rivkin (2009) found only about 0.03 standard deviation gains in California, roughly 3 SAT points.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Illustrates the general scale-up problem: pilot-program benefits often vanish at statewide scale.
insights.quote: mandated CSR in Florida had little, if any, effect on student achievement

insights.claim: Smith argues shrinking class sizes exhausts the limited pool of good teachers and forces hiring of worse ones, canceling potential benefits; California's rollout saw more uncertified, inexperienced teachers, especially in disadvantaged schools.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Class-size mandates can actively degrade teacher quality where it matters most.
insights.quote: Our obsession with shrinking class sizes is causing us to use up the available pool of good teachers, and start hiring bad ones.

insights.claim: Review papers (Jackson et al. 2014; Hanushek and Rivkin 2011) find large positive effects from teacher quality.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Teacher quality is the higher-return lever for education spending.

insights.claim: Given a fixed budget, Smith argues money should go to higher teacher salaries to attract more capable people rather than more teachers, while still spending more on disadvantaged students.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Implies a shift in public education budgets from headcount to compensation, with friction from current staffing mandates.
insights.quote: Our obsession with using budgetary increases to increase the quantity of teachers, rather than to pay teachers more and raise the quality, looks like a miscalculation.

insights.claim: Biasi and Sandholtz (2025) find Wisconsin's law weakening teachers' unions and liberalizing pay cut union revenues, raised test scores, increased some teachers' pay, and raised the incumbent governor's vote share by about 20% of his victory margin.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests pay-for-quality reforms opposed by unions can be both educationally effective and electorally rewarded, lowering their political risk.
insights.quote: the reform cut union revenues, raised student test scores, and increased pay for some teachers
insights.locator: Update: There actually is some research
